read_this_first: The question: the owner's plan in its most favourable form. Show the system what experts did, each thing once, and it has learned it. Here the things are bug fixes, and the number shown is turned up from 3 to 2,864. How many bugs it has never seen does that repair?

The lessons are 2,864 real fixes: Python programs handed in at AtCoder, each as its author first wrote it wrong and then right, one faulty line apart (ConDefects). The bugs are the 100 scored HumanEvalFix bugs. Nobody in this project wrote either. The learner is the edit-kind learner as it stands; at most 200 candidate programs are run against a bug's tests.

Bugs repaired, of 100 (mean of two orders of the lessons): 3 lessons 13.5; 10 lessons 30.5; 30 lessons 36.5; 100 lessons 44.5; 300 lessons 50; 1,000 lessons 56; 2,864 lessons 55. Every tripling of the lessons adds about six bugs up to 1,000 lessons. From 1,000 to 2,864 it adds none.
Right as far as checked, of 100: 3 lessons 9.5; 10 lessons 25.5; 30 lessons 29; 100 lessons 36.5; 300 lessons 42.5; 1,000 lessons 48.5; 2,864 lessons 48.

The control is the same pairs shown backwards, from the correct program to the faulty one: a memory of the same size that holds no fix. It repairs 43 with 100 pairs, 54 with 1,000 and 57 with all, and 34, 45 and 49 of those are right. With all the pairs the memory that holds no fix repairs 2 more bugs than the memory of fixes. What carries over is a stock of small changes; which way a fix goes carries nothing at this size. The tests do the choosing.

Why more stops helping: more lessons reach further and bury what they reach. The published fix is somewhere among the candidates for 40.5 bugs at 1,000 lessons and for 46 with all of them, but among the first 200 candidates for 35 and then 34. The candidates for one bug (the middle bug) go from 12,138 to 30,274.

Lessons from close by are worth about four times as many from far off: the 243 fixes of the benchmark itself and of QuixBugs repaired 56 bugs within 200 candidates, and it takes 1,000 fixes of AtCoder programs to repair 56.

What no amount of this has reached. Over every way without a model that this line of work has measured on these 100 bugs (the learner with four memories and their controls, the tree's repair solver, the stream), 78 bugs were repaired by at least one way and 22 by none. Of those 22, 10 are bugs of missing logic (of 19 such bugs) and 7 of excess logic (of 19): code that has to be written or taken out, not one small change.

What was written down before the run, and what came. Expected: the number repaired rises up to some hundreds of lessons and then stops rising or falls. It rose up to 1,000 and then stopped. Expected: under 62 at the largest dose. It is 55. Expected: the backwards control within 10 of the fixes at the largest dose. It is 2 above them.
One run by the producer on one machine. Nobody else has run it. Zero model calls.

limits: One machine, one producer, one run. Nobody else has run this.
Two orders of the lessons for every dose below all; one order for the control.
At most 200 candidates are run. With more, more bugs are repaired: the benchmark's own fixes repaired 56 within 200 and 62 within 1,000. The flattening is at this budget.
The lessons are whole programs for contest tasks and the bugs are small functions. Another pair of sources may give another curve.
Right 'as far as checked' is not right: the extra inputs are a sample.
'By at least one way' is a count over measurements, not a system. Nothing here knows which way to trust on a given bug.
The count of bugs whose published fix is among the candidates looks for that one program; other right repairs are not counted there.

The 100 bugs had been scored before in other measurements of this learner. The learner was frozen before they were first scored and has not been changed; the tool of this measurement was frozen before it ran on them.
The learner applies no operator that would make more than 300 candidates in a program; that cap is part of what is measured.
